newsitem.title: UK: Claims validation still problem for UK gas industry.
newsitem.headline: Claims validation still problem for UK gas industry.

text.p: Claims validation in gas trading, the process by which producers and shippers of gas offshore measure volumes before they come ashore at beach terminals, is still seriously flawed and undermining the developing U.K. gas market, a conference heard on Tuesday.

Maria Foster, gas trading manager at National Power Plc who is also the chair of the management committee of Claims Validation Services Limited (CVSL), said there were several problems preventing effective claims validation from taking place.
"TransCo (the British Gas Plc unit responsible for onshore pipelines) successfully argued that validation was a shipper and trader issue, and it has not got involved," she said.

"So CVSL now consists of shippers, traders, and some trading producers. It has two agents, the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) and Coopers and Lybrand, appointed before the Network Code started in March. The six beach terminals are divided between them, with each responsible for three.
"Claims validation should be straightforward. The lines of communication betwen principals and agents are clearly defined, but they are not being followed," Foster said.
The biggest problem is that producers are not offering accurate data about the amount of gas they produce.
But Foster said an initiative between the regulator Ofgas and the Department of Trade and Industry offered "some hope" that this will soon be resolved.
Another problem is that all data is transmitted by fax, rather than electronically, and deadlines are not observed.
"Sometimes literally thousands of faxes come in changing submissions after deadlines have passed", she said.
Some of these changes in submissions are the result of "after the day trading", which is in any case contrary to the Network Code, Foster said.

The danger is that if CVSL is not able to supply accurate data, reconciling what producers claim they have supplied and what actually flows through beach terminals, the industry will have to turn instead to a compromise offered by the Network Code default procedure.
"This has no facility for a challenge", Foster said.
She added that CVSL needed to introduce majority voting to allow changes. At present a vote of 100 percent of CVSL members is needed, and this was "unworkable", although this is now being addressed.
The IPE, whose plans to launch a series of forward gas contracts based at beach terminals are being thwarted by the problems of claims validation, is the highest profile victim of the CVSL.
"I understand the IPE's frustration at not being able to launch a beach contract," Foster said. "We cannot continue to move at the pace of the slowest boat in the convoy."
